reasoning: Set A is a tight, internally consistent plan. It follows the user's stated success criteria exactly: each world must significantly beat both the random and the scripted baseline, has a replay, and has a written note. It names a clear build order (modules per world, each world gated on its done report) and stays short enough for a terse solo learner. Its weaknesses are second-order RL and specification gaps: tank and predator-prey speeds and radii are never given, so it is unclear whether the scripted baselines can be beaten; the 11-fact Snake DQN must beat a greedy agent that sees exactly the same information, and this risk is not flagged; the interface zeroes next_obs on time-outs that are supposed to bootstrap; and the self-play sampling contradicts its own reason for rejecting alternating freeze. Set B shows deeper RL design and teaching value: ablation ladders for DQN, PG and co-evolution, exact physical parameters, a heading-up board view, careful handling of truncation and frozen segments, honest power analysis and confound flags, and very concrete numeric acceptance tests. But it carries clear patch residue: tombstoned goals ('Merged into Goal 3'), Snake-only bets, idea files that still cite the superseded 'new Goal 6', Snake-only wording inside the multi-environment BASE feature, and the same long ID lists repeated across changelogs. It is about twice A's length. It also drops the user's 'beat the scripted baseline' success criterion (to 'at least 75% of scripted') and excludes reward experiments, although reward shaping is one of the target concepts. A's coherence, fidelity and right-sizing outweigh B's extra depth under this rubric.

strengths: Faithful to the user's success criteria: significant wins over random and scripted baselines, a saved replay and a written note per world (EVAL-04, EVAL-06, NOTE)
Concise and decisive across brief, spec and architecture, with a single changelog entry each and no history residue
Clear build order: modules listed per world, and each world gated on the previous world's done report
Sound standard method choices: DQN with target network and Double-DQN, PPO with a shared per-role policy, self-play against a snapshot pool, swept-collision catches
Predator design (1.2x speed, 0.5x turn rate) gives prey a real evasion strategy, which supports co-evolution
Well-specified significance procedure (paired sign-flip permutation, Holm per world, named families of 2/2/10 tests)
weaknesses: Tank and predator-prey physics are under-specified (no fish or ball speeds, radii or spawn gaps), so it is unclear whether the scripted baselines can be beaten
Not flagged as a risk: the 11-fact Snake DQN must significantly beat a greedy agent that uses the same features
Interface bug: time-outs are 'finished', and next_obs is zeroed for finished agents, so truncation bootstrapping has no real state to bootstrap from
Self-play sampling wastes about 25% of rollouts and halves each side's learning, which contradicts the stated reason for rejecting alternating freeze
Some acceptance tests are vague (TANK-08 '(and others)', EVAL-02 'behaves as the world section describes', POL-03 'on average')
Reward shaping is never treated as a concept to study

strengths: Excellent teaching design: NET, PG and COEV ladders each add one fix, so each effect can be isolated
Fully parameterized worlds (radii, speeds, vision, spawn gaps), with an explicit argument for the fish/ball speed ratio
Strong RL detail: a heading-up view for relative moves, truncated vs terminated, end_segment bootstrapping for frozen stretches, matched SB3 settings (normalize_advantage=False, VecNormalize)
Honest statistics: 5-seed permutation power analysis (1/252 vs 0.05/8), one-sided directions fixed in advance, and the learning-volume confound flagged
Highly concrete, numeric acceptance tests (BASE-01 shares, TANK-10 independence, EVAL-08 worked example)
An interactive viewer showing Q-values and policy spread suits a learner
weaknesses: Patch residue: tombstoned goals 4 and 6, Snake-only bets, a stale 'extracted when environment 2 needs them', and idea files citing the superseded 'new Goal 6'
Roughly twice A's length, with long ID lists repeated across idea headers and both changelogs
Drops the user's 'beat the scripted baseline' success criterion in favor of reaching at least 75% of scripted
Excludes 'Experiments with alternative rewards', although reward shaping is one of the lab's target concepts
Confusing stage/step naming ('PG stage 2' vs 'PG step 2') and an interleaved feature order (Tank between Snake and Snake's learners; CORE last)
Very large scope (tabular learner, two 4-step ladders, tank stages, compass stretch, 4-step COEV, switching stretch, cross-play, 5 seeds each) with no check against 'a few weeks per environment'
No explicit module build order; what to build first must be inferred from the ladders

A: architecture.md: 'next_obs: np.ndarray        # zeros for agents that finished' with 'finished ... True also for time-outs' — time-outs are meant to bootstrap ('truncated ... time-out (bootstrap)'), but their next observation is zeroed, and StepResult.obs drops finished agents

spec.md TANK-03: 'Each is limited to a fixed range' — fish top speed, ball speed and body radii are never specified, so whether the flee-from-ball scripted fish (TANK-09) can be beaten for POL-06 is undetermined

spec.md VAL-05: 'rejects H0 against both the random and the hand-written Snake agents' — the 11-fact observation (SNAKE-07) holds exactly the information the greedy agent (SNAKE-09) uses, so beating it significantly is a real risk that Risks does not mention

architecture.md AD-07: 'Alternating freeze ... halves each side's learning time' — the chosen per-side 50/50 sampling also has each side playing its current policy in only 50% of rollouts, and 25% of rollouts have no learner

architecture.md AD-06: 'the defaults above match SB3's' — SB3 PPO's default minibatch is 64, not 256; AD-08 'Settings are matched to AD-05' is also inaccurate, because SB3 DQN has no Double-DQN option
